q: Under Article 1700 of the Civil Code, the relations between capital and labor are:
choices: Not merely contractual, but impressed with public interest, so labor contracts must yield to the common good
Governed only by the parties' agreement
hints: Labor contracts are subject to special labor laws.
Parties cannot contract away statutory labor rights.
why: The main sources of Philippine labor law are the 1987 Constitution (Art. II, Sec. 18; Art. XIII, Sec. 3), the Labor Code, and the Civil Code (Arts. 1700-1702). Under Civil Code Art. 1700, labor contracts are impressed with public interest.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 3; Civil Code, Arts. 1700-1702

q: An employment contract signed by a worker provided that he would receive no overtime pay and could be dismissed at any time without cause, "as freely agreed by the parties." Is the contract valid?

alac.answer: No, those stipulations are void.
alac.basis: Article 1700 of the Civil Code provides that the relations between capital and labor are not merely contractual; they are so impressed with public interest that labor contracts must yield to the common good, and are subject to special laws on wages, working conditions and the like. Article XIII, Section 3 of the Constitution guarantees workers security of tenure and just and humane conditions of work, and the Labor Code grants overtime pay and protects security of tenure.
alac.application: Here, the waiver of overtime pay and the clause allowing dismissal without cause contravene the Labor Code and the constitutional guarantee of security of tenure. The parties' freedom of contract cannot override these laws.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, those stipulations are void, and the worker is entitled to overtime pay and protection against dismissal without just or authorized cause.

keyPoints: Labor relations impressed with public interest (Civil Code Art. 1700)
Constitutional and statutory rights cannot be waived by contract
Sources: Constitution, Labor Code, Civil Code
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 3; Civil Code, Arts. 1700-1702

q: Ratified ILO Conventions, such as Convention No. 87 on freedom of association, form part of Philippine law:
choices: As treaties concurred in by the Senate, and they guide the interpretation of labor laws
Only if the DOLE adopts them
hints: The Philippines has ratified the core ILO conventions.
They are applied together with the Labor Code.
why: Ratified ILO conventions are treaties that become part of the law of the land upon Senate concurrence (Const. Art. VII, Sec. 21), and the Constitution adopts generally accepted principles of international law (Art. II, Sec. 2); they are sources of labor law and guide interpretation.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 2; ILO Convention No. 87 (Freedom of Association)

q: A union argues that a DOLE rule requiring unions to have at least 20% of employees before registering violates ILO Convention No. 87, which the Philippines ratified. What is the legal status of the Convention in the dispute?

alac.answer: The Convention is part of Philippine law and may be invoked to interpret or challenge the rule, which must be harmonized with it.
alac.basis: Under Article II, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution, the Philippines adopts the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the land, and treaties concurred in by the Senate become part of domestic law. ILO Convention No. 87, on freedom of association and protection of the right to organize, has been ratified by the Philippines. It is a source of labor law and is used to interpret statutes and rules on self-organization.
alac.application: Here, the union invokes a ratified ILO Convention against a DOLE rule. The Convention has the force of a statute, so the rule must be consistent with it and with the Labor Code it implements.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the union may invoke the Convention, and the rule should be struck down or read narrowly if it unduly restricts the freedom of association.

keyPoints: Ratified ILO conventions are part of Philippine law
Constitution adopts generally accepted principles of international law
Used to interpret labor rules
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 2; ILO Convention No. 87 (Freedom of Association)

q: DOLE issuances, such as Department Orders and implementing rules:
choices: Implement the Labor Code and have the force of law, but cannot expand or contradict the law
hints: Administrative rules must be within the law.
Doubts in implementing rules favor labor (Art. 4).
why: The Labor Code authorizes the DOLE to issue rules and regulations; such issuances are sources of labor law but cannot go beyond or contradict the statute they implement; doubts in the Code and its implementing rules are resolved in favor of labor (Art. 4).
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 5

q: A DOLE Department Order added a requirement, not found in the Labor Code, that a worker must have served at least five years before claiming holiday pay. A worker with two years of service claims holiday pay. Should the Order prevail?

alac.answer: No, the Order cannot prevail over the Labor Code.
alac.basis: DOLE issuances implement the Labor Code and are sources of labor law, but administrative rules cannot add to, amend or contradict the law they implement. Article 4 of the Labor Code also provides that all doubts in the implementation and interpretation of the Code, including its implementing rules and regulations, shall be resolved in favor of labor.
alac.application: Here, the Labor Code grants holiday pay without a five-year service requirement. The Department Order adds a restriction that the law does not provide, to the prejudice of workers.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the requirement is invalid, and the worker is entitled to holiday pay.

keyPoints: DOLE issuances implement but cannot expand the law
Doubts in implementing rules resolved in favor of labor (Art. 4)
Statute prevails over inconsistent rules
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 5

q: In Calalang v. Williams, social justice was described as:
choices: The humanization of laws and the equalization of social and economic forces by the State, so that justice in its rational and objectively secular conception may be approximated
Favoring the poor in every case
hints: Social justice does not mean always ruling for labor.
It operates within the law.
why: Art. II, Sec. 10: the State shall promote social justice in all phases of national development; Calalang v. Williams, G.R. No. 47800, December 2, 1940, defined social justice as the humanization of laws and the equalization of social and economic forces. Social justice does not justify ignoring the law or the rights of employers.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 10; Calalang v. Williams, G.R. No. 47800, December 2, 1940

q: A labor arbiter ruled for a dismissed employee solely because "social justice favors the poor," even though the evidence clearly showed the employee committed serious theft. Is the ruling correct?

alac.answer: No, the ruling is not correct.
alac.basis: Article II, Section 10 of the 1987 Constitution directs the State to promote social justice in all phases of national development. In Calalang v. Williams, G.R. No. 47800, December 2, 1940, the Supreme Court described social justice as the humanization of laws and the equalization of social and economic forces, so that justice may be approximated. Social justice does not authorize the courts to disregard the law and the evidence; it cannot be used to shield wrongdoing by employees.
alac.application: Here, the evidence clearly established that the employee committed serious theft, which is a just cause for dismissal. Social justice cannot be invoked to protect him from the consequences of his misconduct.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the ruling should be reversed, and the dismissal upheld if due process was observed.

keyPoints: Social justice in all phases of development (Art. II, Sec. 10)
Definition in Calalang v. Williams
Not a license to ignore law and evidence
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 10; Calalang v. Williams, G.R. No. 47800, December 2, 1940

q: Under Article II, Section 18 of the 1987 Constitution, the State affirms labor as:
choices: A primary social economic force, and shall protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare
hints: Declaration of principles guide policy.
Specific rights come from Art. XIII and statutes.
why: Art. II, Sec. 18: labor is a primary social economic force; the State protects workers' rights and welfare. It is a state policy guiding legislation and interpretation, not by itself a source of enforceable rights.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 18

q: A worker sued his employer directly under Article II, Section 18 of the Constitution, claiming a right to a salary increase because "labor is a primary social economic force." No law or contract grants the increase. Will his claim prosper?

alac.answer: No, the claim will not prosper.
alac.basis: Article II, Section 18 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State affirms labor as a primary social economic force and shall protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. As a declaration of state policy, it is generally not self-executing; it guides the legislature and the courts in interpreting laws but does not by itself create a judicially enforceable right to specific benefits.
alac.application: Here, the worker relies solely on Article II, Section 18 for a salary increase, without any law, wage order or contract granting it.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, his claim has no legal basis, although the policy may guide the interpretation of laws in his favor in proper cases.

keyPoints: Labor as a primary social economic force (Art. II, Sec. 18)
State policies are generally not self-executing
Specific rights must rest on law or contract
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. II, Sec. 18

q: Under Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution, the State shall afford full protection to labor:
choices: Local and overseas, organized and unorganized
hints: The same section recognizes employers' rights.
It covers OFWs.
why: Art. XIII, Sec. 3 extends full protection to all labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized; it also recognizes the right of employers to reasonable returns on investments, so protection to labor does not mean oppression of capital.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3

q: A Filipino seafarer, not a union member, was denied death benefits by his foreign employer, which argued that constitutional labor protection covers only local unionized workers. Is the employer correct?

alac.answer: No, the employer is not correct.
alac.basis: Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall afford full protection to labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized, and promote full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all. The same section also recognizes the right of enterprises to reasonable returns on investments.
alac.application: Here, the seafarer is an overseas worker who is not unionized. Both categories are expressly covered by the constitutional mandate of full protection to labor.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the seafarer is entitled to the protection of the Constitution and the applicable laws and contracts on death benefits.

keyPoints: Full protection to labor (Art. XIII, Sec. 3)
Covers overseas and unorganized workers
Balanced with employers' right to reasonable returns
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3

q: Security of tenure means that:
choices: An employee may be dismissed only for a just or authorized cause and after due process
No employee may ever be dismissed
hints: It is a constitutional right.
Probationary employees enjoy it during the probationary period.
why: Security of tenure (Const. Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code Art. 3) protects employees from dismissal except for just or authorized causes provided by law and with due process; it applies to regular employees and, within their terms, to probationary and fixed-term employees.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 3

q: A company dismissed a regular employee with 10 years of service, with no reason given, paying him three months' salary "as a courtesy." Is the dismissal valid?

alac.answer: No, the dismissal is illegal.
alac.basis: Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution guarantees workers security of tenure, and Article 3 of the Labor Code provides that the State shall assure the rights of workers to security of tenure. An employee may be dismissed only for a just or authorized cause provided by law and after observance of due process.
alac.application: Here, the employer dismissed a regular employee without any cause. Paying three months' salary does not cure the lack of a lawful cause.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the dismissal is illegal, and the employee is entitled to reinstatement with full backwages (or separation pay in lieu of reinstatement when proper).

keyPoints: Security of tenure (Const. Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code Art. 3)
Dismissal only for just or authorized cause with due process
Payment of salary does not cure illegality
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 3

q: In International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing, the Supreme Court held that paying foreign-hired teachers higher salaries than local-hired teachers for the same work:
choices: Violates the principle of equal pay for equal work
Is valid because of their nationality
Is a management prerogative without limit
hints: Equal work deserves equal pay.
Distinctions must rest on reasonable grounds.
why: Equal employment opportunity (Const. Art. XIII, Sec. 3; Labor Code Art. 3) and equal pay for equal work mean employees performing equal work with equal skill, effort and responsibility should be paid equally; a higher salary based on foreign hiring alone is discriminatory (ISAE v. Quisumbing, G.R. No. 128845, June 1, 2000). Housing and travel allowances for foreign hires may be justified.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3; International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing, G.R. No. 128845, June 1, 2000

q: A school paid its foreign-hired teachers 25% more salary than its local-hired teachers who held the same positions and performed the same duties, citing the foreign hires' "dislocation factor." Is the salary difference valid?

alac.answer: No, the salary difference is not valid, although allowances for the dislocation factor may be.
alac.basis: Article 3 of the Labor Code and Article XIII, Section 3 of the Constitution ensure equal work opportunities and promote equality of employment opportunities. In International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing, G.R. No. 128845, June 1, 2000, the Supreme Court held that persons who work with substantially equal qualifications, skill, effort and responsibility under similar conditions should be paid similar salaries, and that the dislocation factor of foreign hires is properly addressed by benefits such as housing and travel allowances, not a higher basic salary.
alac.application: Here, the local-hired and foreign-hired teachers hold the same positions and perform the same duties. The dislocation factor does not justify a higher basic salary.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the salary difference is discriminatory, although the school may give the foreign hires appropriate allowances.

keyPoints: Equal employment opportunity (Art. 3; Const. Art. XIII, Sec. 3)
Equal pay for equal work (ISAE v. Quisumbing)
Dislocation factor addressed by allowances, not salary
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3; International School Alliance of Educators v. Quisumbing, G.R. No. 128845, June 1, 2000

q: Under Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution, the right to strike is:
choices: Guaranteed, but must be exercised in accordance with law
hints: Strikes must comply with the Labor Code's procedural requirements.
Government employees may not strike.
why: Art. XIII, Sec. 3 guarantees the rights to self-organization, collective bargaining and negotiations, and peaceful concerted activities, including the right to strike in accordance with law; Art. III, Sec. 8 protects the right to form unions. Government employees may organize but may not strike.
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3

q: A company required all newly hired employees to sign an undertaking that they would never join a union, as a condition of employment. Is the undertaking valid?

alac.answer: No, the undertaking is void.
alac.basis: Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution guarantees the rights of all workers to self-organization, collective bargaining and negotiations, and peaceful concerted activities, including the right to strike in accordance with law. The Labor Code also makes it an unfair labor practice to require as a condition of employment that a person shall not join a labor organization (yellow-dog contract).
alac.application: Here, the company conditioned employment on a promise not to join any union, which directly restrains the constitutional right to self-organization.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the undertaking is void, and imposing it is an unfair labor practice.

keyPoints: Right to self-organization and collective bargaining (Art. XIII, Sec. 3)
Yellow-dog contracts are prohibited
Right to strike in accordance with law
cite: 1987 Constitution, Art. XIII, Sec. 3

q: Under Article 1702 of the Civil Code and Article 4 of the Labor Code, doubts in labor legislation and contracts are resolved:
choices: In favor of labor (the safety and decent living of the laborer)
hints: It applies only when there is real doubt.
Clear provisions are applied as written.
why: Civil Code Art. 1702: labor legislation and contracts are construed in favor of the safety and decent living of the laborer; Labor Code Art. 4: doubts in the Code and its rules are resolved in favor of labor. The rule applies only when there is genuine doubt.
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1702; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 4

q: A collective bargaining agreement grants a "rice allowance to all employees." The employer says probationary employees are excluded; the union says they are included. The CBA is silent. How should the doubt be resolved?

alac.answer: The doubt should be resolved in favor of the probationary employees, who are entitled to the rice allowance.
alac.basis: Article 1702 of the Civil Code provides that in case of doubt, all labor legislation and all labor contracts shall be construed in favor of the safety and decent living for the laborer. Article 4 of the Labor Code likewise provides that all doubts in the implementation and interpretation of its provisions shall be resolved in favor of labor. A CBA is a labor contract.
alac.application: Here, the CBA grants the allowance to "all employees" and does not exclude probationary employees. To the extent there is doubt, it must be resolved in favor of the workers.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the probationary employees are entitled to the rice allowance.

keyPoints: Labor contracts construed in favor of the laborer (Civil Code Art. 1702)
Doubts resolved in favor of labor (Labor Code Art. 4)
CBA is a labor contract
cite: Civil Code, Art. 1702; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 4

q: According to People v. Panis, the proviso in Article 13(b) of the Labor Code that offering employment for a fee to two or more persons is deemed recruitment:
choices: Creates a presumption; dealing with even one person can be recruitment
Means recruiting one person is never recruitment
hints: Profit is not an element.
Referrals and advertising are included.
why: Labor Code Art. 13(b) defines recruitment and placement broadly, whether for profit or not, locally or abroad; the proviso on two or more persons only creates a presumption, so recruiting even one person may suffice (People v. Panis, G.R. Nos. L-58674-77, July 11, 1990).
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 13(b); People v. Panis, G.R. Nos. L-58674-77, July 11, 1990

q: Without any license, Marie told her neighbor, a single person, that she could get him a job in Dubai and collected P50,000 as "processing fee." She argues that she cannot be guilty of recruitment because she dealt with only one person. Is she correct?

alac.answer: No, Marie engaged in recruitment and placement.
alac.basis: Article 13(b) of the Labor Code defines recruitment and placement as any act of canvassing, enlisting, contracting, transporting, utilizing, hiring or procuring workers, including promising or advertising for employment, locally or abroad, whether for profit or not, and provides that any person who offers or promises for a fee employment to two or more persons shall be deemed engaged in recruitment. In People v. Panis, G.R. Nos. L-58674-77, July 11, 1990, the Supreme Court held that the proviso merely creates a presumption, and that dealing with only one person can constitute recruitment.
alac.application: Here, Marie promised her neighbor a job abroad and collected a fee. That act is recruitment, even though it involved only one person.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Marie engaged in recruitment and placement; as a non-licensee, she is liable for illegal recruitment.

keyPoints: Recruitment and placement defined (Art. 13(b))
Two-person proviso only a presumption (People v. Panis)
Profit not required
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 13(b); People v. Panis, G.R. Nos. L-58674-77, July 11, 1990

q: Under Article 40 of the Labor Code, an alien employment permit may be issued after a determination that:
choices: No person in the Philippines is competent, able and willing to perform the services for which the alien is desired
hints: This is the labor market test.
Some aliens are exempt or excluded under DOLE rules.
why: Labor Code Art. 40: aliens seeking employment, and employers hiring them, must obtain an employment permit from DOLE, issued after a labor market test showing no available competent, able and willing Filipino; DO 248, as amended, governs the procedure.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 40; DOLE Department Order No. 248, as amended

q: A call center hired a foreign national as a customer service agent without an alien employment permit, though many Filipinos applied for the same job. When the DOLE found out, the company argued that it may hire whomever it wants. Is the company correct?

alac.answer: No, the company is not correct.
alac.basis: Article 40 of the Labor Code requires any alien seeking admission to the Philippines for employment purposes, and any employer who desires to engage an alien, to obtain an employment permit from the Department of Labor, which may be issued only after a determination of the non-availability of a person in the Philippines who is competent, able and willing to perform the services for which the alien is desired.
alac.application: Here, the company hired the foreign national without a permit, and the job could clearly be done by the many qualified Filipino applicants, so the labor market test would not be met.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the employment violates Article 40 and DO 248, and the company may be penalized.

keyPoints: Alien employment permit (Art. 40)
Labor market test: no available Filipino
Management prerogative limited by law
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 40; DOLE Department Order No. 248, as amended

q: Under Article 16 of the Labor Code, as a rule, recruitment and placement of workers is done by:
choices: Public employment offices, except as allowed for licensed or authorized private entities
hints: Public employment offices do not charge fees.
Private entities need a license or authority.
why: Labor Code Art. 16: recruitment and placement is reserved to public employment offices, except for private entities licensed or authorized under Chapter II (Art. 25); Public Employment Service Offices (PESOs) provide free employment facilitation services under RA 8759.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Arts. 14-16

q: A town mayor set up a municipal office that refers unemployed residents to local factories for free. A private agency complained that the municipal office needs a DOLE license. Is the private agency correct?

alac.answer: No, the municipal office, as a public employment office, does not need a license.
alac.basis: Article 16 of the Labor Code provides that, except as provided in Chapter II of the Title, no person or entity other than the public employment offices shall engage in the recruitment and placement of workers. The license or authority requirement applies to private employment entities, while public employment offices, such as the Public Employment Service Offices established by LGUs, are authorized by law to provide employment facilitation services.
alac.application: Here, the mayor's office is a public employment office providing free referrals. The license requirement applies only to private recruiters.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the municipal office may operate without a DOLE license.

keyPoints: Recruitment reserved to public employment offices (Art. 16)
Private recruiters need license or authority
PESOs provide free services
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Arts. 14-16

q: Under Article 13 of the Labor Code, a private recruitment entity differs from a private fee-charging employment agency because it:
choices: Does not charge any fee, directly or indirectly, and operates under an authority rather than a license
hints: License = fee-charging agency.
Authority = non-fee-charging entity.
why: Labor Code Art. 13: a private fee-charging employment agency recruits for a fee and needs a license; a private recruitment entity recruits without charging fees and needs an authority. Both are regulated by DOLE (local) or DMW (overseas).
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 13(c)-(f)

q: A company that hires workers for its own factory abroad advertised for Filipino workers and charged no fee. A government officer insists it must obtain a license like a fee-charging agency. What does it need?

alac.answer: It needs an authority as a private recruitment entity, not a license.
alac.basis: Article 13 of the Labor Code defines a private fee-charging employment agency as any person or entity engaged in recruitment and placement for a fee, which requires a license, and a private recruitment entity as any person or association engaged in recruitment and placement without charging, directly or indirectly, any fee from workers or employers, which requires an authority.
alac.application: Here, the company recruits workers for its own needs and charges no fee. It is a private recruitment entity.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, it must obtain an authority, not a license, before recruiting.

keyPoints: Private fee-charging employment agency: license (Art. 13)
Private recruitment entity: no fee; authority
Both need DOLE or DMW approval
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 13(c)-(f)

q: Under Article 29 of the Labor Code, a recruitment license:
choices: Cannot be used by any person other than the licensee, or at any place other than that stated, and cannot be transferred
May be sold to another agency
hints: Branch offices need prior approval.
Use by another makes the user a non-licensee.
why: Labor Code Art. 29: licenses and authorities are non-transferable; any change of address, agents or additional offices needs prior DOLE approval; a person using another's license is a non-licensee for purposes of illegal recruitment.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 29

q: Agency A, a licensed recruiter, allowed Bert, who has no license, to recruit workers for overseas jobs in his own office in Cebu "under" Agency A's license, sharing the fees. Is Bert liable for illegal recruitment?

alac.answer: Yes, Bert is liable for illegal recruitment, and Agency A violated the non-transferability rule.
alac.basis: Article 29 of the Labor Code provides that no license or authority shall be used directly or indirectly by any person other than the one in whose favor it was issued or at any place other than that stated in the license, nor shall it be transferred, conveyed or assigned to any other person or entity, and that additional offices require the prior approval of the DOLE. Recruitment by a non-licensee is illegal recruitment under Article 38.
alac.application: Here, Bert used Agency A's license in his own office, without being the licensee and without DOLE approval for a Cebu office. He is effectively a non-licensee.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Bert is liable for illegal recruitment, and Agency A may have its license suspended or cancelled.

keyPoints: Non-transferability of license (Art. 29)
Use by another person or at an unapproved place prohibited
User is a non-licensee liable for illegal recruitment
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 29

q: Under Article 35 of the Labor Code, the Secretary of Labor (now also the DMW for overseas recruitment) may suspend or cancel a recruitment license for:
choices: Violation of the law or of the rules and regulations governing recruitment
hints: Due process must be observed.
Overseas recruitment is now regulated by the DMW.
why: Labor Code Art. 35 (and RA 11641 for overseas recruitment) empowers the Secretary to suspend or cancel licenses or authorities for violations of laws and rules; Art. 36-37 give regulatory and visitorial powers.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 35

q: The DMW cancelled a recruitment agency's license after finding that it charged workers fees beyond the allowed schedule. The agency argues that only courts can impose sanctions. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, the DMW may cancel the license after due process.
alac.basis: Article 35 of the Labor Code gives the Secretary of Labor the power to suspend or cancel any license or authority to recruit for violation of rules and regulations or of the Labor Code and other applicable laws. RA 11641 transferred the regulation of overseas recruitment to the Department of Migrant Workers. Charging fees greater than the schedule of allowable fees is a prohibited practice under Article 34.
alac.application: Here, the agency charged fees beyond the allowed schedule, a prohibited practice. The DMW, which regulates overseas recruitment, has administrative power to cancel the license after notice and hearing.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the cancellation is valid if the agency was given due process, without prejudice to criminal liability.

keyPoints: Power to suspend or cancel licenses (Art. 35)
Overseas recruitment regulated by the DMW (RA 11641)
Excessive fees are prohibited (Art. 34)
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 35

q: Under RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022, an overseas Filipino worker is a person who:
choices: Only works in the Middle East
Is to be engaged, is engaged, or has been engaged in a remunerated activity in a state of which he or she is not a citizen, or on board a vessel navigating foreign seas
hints: Seafarers are included.
Prospective and former OFWs are covered.
why: RA 8042 Sec. 3(a), as amended by RA 10022, defines OFW (or migrant worker) to include those about to be engaged, currently engaged, or previously engaged in remunerated activity abroad or on foreign-going vessels or offshore installations.
cite: Migrant Workers Act (RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022), Sec. 3(a)

q: Carla signed a contract to work as a nurse in Saudi Arabia but was never deployed because her agency failed to process her papers. She filed a money claim under RA 8042. The agency argues she is not an OFW since she never left. Is it correct?

alac.answer: No, Carla is an OFW under RA 8042, as amended.
alac.basis: Section 3(a) of RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022, defines an overseas Filipino worker as a person who is to be engaged, is engaged or has been engaged in a remunerated activity in a state of which he or she is not a citizen, or on board a vessel navigating the foreign seas.
alac.application: Here, Carla signed a contract to work in Saudi Arabia; she is a person who "is to be engaged" in remunerated activity abroad, even though she was not deployed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Carla is an OFW entitled to the protection and remedies of RA 8042, as amended.

keyPoints: OFW defined (RA 8042, Sec. 3(a), as amended)
Includes those 'to be engaged'
Covered by the Act's protections
cite: Migrant Workers Act (RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022), Sec. 3(a)

q: Under Article 27 of the Labor Code, to participate in the recruitment and placement of workers, a corporation must be:
choices: At least 75% owned and controlled by Filipino citizens
hints: This is stricter than the general 60-40 rule.
RA 10022 also bars non-Filipinos from heading or managing agencies.
why: Labor Code Arts. 25-27: the private sector participates in recruitment under DOLE (now DMW for overseas) rules; only Filipino citizens or entities at least 75% Filipino-owned may engage in recruitment; overseas, both fee-charging agencies (license) and non-fee recruitment entities (authority) are regulated.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Arts. 13 and 25-27

q: A corporation 70% owned by Filipinos and 30% by Japanese nationals applied for a license to recruit Filipino workers for jobs in Japan. Should the license be granted?

alac.answer: No, the license should be denied.
alac.basis: Article 27 of the Labor Code provides that only Filipino citizens or corporations, partnerships or entities at least seventy-five percent of the authorized and voting capital stock of which is owned and controlled by Filipino citizens shall be permitted to participate in the recruitment and placement of workers, locally or overseas.
alac.application: Here, the corporation is only 70% Filipino-owned, below the 75% required.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, it does not qualify for a recruitment license unless its Filipino ownership is increased to at least 75%.

keyPoints: Private sector participation in recruitment (Art. 25)
Citizenship requirement: at least 75% Filipino (Art. 27)
License or authority required
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Arts. 13 and 25-27

q: Under Section 10 of RA 8042, as amended, the liability of the foreign employer and the local recruitment agency for an OFW's money claims is:
hints: Corporate officers of the agency are also solidarily liable.
The performance bond answers for claims.
why: RA 8042 Sec. 10, as amended by RA 10022: the principal/employer and the agency are jointly and severally liable for OFW claims; corporate officers and directors of the agency are also solidarily liable; the liability continues for the duration of the contract and is not affected by substitution or amendment of the contract.
cite: Migrant Workers Act (RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022), Sec. 10

q: An OFW was illegally dismissed by her employer in Hong Kong. She sued both the foreign employer and the Philippine agency that deployed her. The agency argues that only the foreign employer, which fired her, is liable. Is the agency correct?

alac.answer: No, the agency is solidarily liable with the foreign employer.
alac.basis: Section 10 of RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022, provides that the liability of the principal/employer and the recruitment/placement agency for any and all claims arising out of the employer-employee relationship shall be joint and several, that this shall be a condition precedent for the approval of the overseas employment contract, and that the corporate officers and directors of the agency shall themselves be jointly and solidarily liable with the corporation.
alac.application: Here, the OFW's claim arises from her illegal dismissal by the foreign employer. The Philippine agency that deployed her is, by law, jointly and severally liable with the employer.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the OFW may recover the full amount from the agency, which may seek reimbursement from the foreign employer.

keyPoints: Joint and several liability of agency and employer (RA 8042, Sec. 10, as amended)
Condition for approval of the contract
Corporate officers also solidarily liable
cite: Migrant Workers Act (RA 8042, as amended by RA 10022), Sec. 10

q: Under the principle of imputed knowledge in overseas employment, the local agency is liable because:
choices: The agent's knowledge is imputed to the principal and vice versa, so the agency cannot claim ignorance of the foreign employer's acts
hints: The agency and the employer are principal and agent.
The OFW need not sue abroad.
why: As agent of the foreign employer, the local agency is deemed to know what its principal knows, and vice versa; together with the solidary liability under RA 8042 Sec. 10, the agency cannot escape liability by claiming ignorance of the employer's acts (Sameer Overseas Placement Agency v. Cabiles, G.R. No. 170139, August 5, 2014).
cite: Sameer Overseas Placement Agency, Inc. v. Cabiles, G.R. No. 170139, August 5, 2014; RA 8042, as amended, Sec. 10

q: A foreign employer dismissed an OFW, citing "inefficiency," without informing the local agency. When sued, the agency argued that it had no knowledge of the dismissal or its reasons. Is that a valid defense?

alac.answer: No, the agency's lack of knowledge is not a defense.
alac.basis: In Sameer Overseas Placement Agency, Inc. v. Cabiles, G.R. No. 170139, August 5, 2014, the Supreme Court explained that the local agency is jointly and solidarily liable with the foreign employer, and that, as the agent of the foreign principal, the knowledge of the principal is imputed to the agency. Section 10 of RA 8042, as amended, makes the agency's joint and several liability a condition for the approval of the overseas contract.
alac.application: Here, the agency, as agent of the foreign employer, is deemed to know of the dismissal and its grounds. It cannot avoid liability by claiming it was not informed.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the agency is liable with the foreign employer for the illegal dismissal, unless the dismissal is shown to be valid.

keyPoints: Agent and principal: imputed knowledge
Solidary liability under RA 8042, Sec. 10
Sameer Overseas Placement Agency v. Cabiles
cite: Sameer Overseas Placement Agency, Inc. v. Cabiles, G.R. No. 170139, August 5, 2014; RA 8042, as amended, Sec. 10

q: Under Article 26 of the Labor Code, which of the following may NOT engage in recruitment for overseas employment?
choices: A private recruitment entity with authority
Travel agencies and sales agencies of airline companies
hints: The prohibition applies even if no profit is made.
It prevents conflicts of interest.
why: Labor Code Art. 26 bars travel agencies and airline sales agencies from overseas recruitment, whether for profit or not; RA 8042, as amended, also bars certain government officials and employees and their relatives from engaging in overseas recruitment.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 26

q: A licensed travel agency offered a package including a job placement in Canada, a visa and plane tickets, charging P150,000. Is this allowed?

alac.answer: No; the travel agency may not engage in recruitment for overseas employment.
alac.basis: Article 26 of the Labor Code provides that travel agencies and sales agencies of airline companies are prohibited from engaging in the business of recruitment and placement of workers for overseas employment, whether for profit or not. A travel agency's license to sell tickets is not a license to recruit.
alac.application: Here, the travel agency offered job placement in Canada as part of its package, which is recruitment and placement for overseas employment.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the travel agency violated Article 26 and, as a non-licensee for recruitment, may be liable for illegal recruitment.

keyPoints: Travel agencies prohibited from overseas recruitment (Art. 26)
Whether for profit or not
Recruitment without license is illegal recruitment
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 26

q: For overseas recruitment, opening an additional branch office of a licensed agency requires:
choices: The prior approval of the DOLE (now the DMW)
hints: Agents and representatives must be approved.
The license covers only the approved place.
why: Labor Code Art. 29 (applied to overseas recruitment, now administered by the DMW): licenses are non-transferable, and transfers of address, designation of agents and additional offices require prior approval; recruitment through an unapproved office or agent may be illegal recruitment.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 29; RA 8042, as amended

q: A licensed overseas recruitment agency in Manila opened an unapproved satellite office in Davao, where its agent collected fees from applicants. Is the activity in Davao lawful?

alac.answer: No; the Davao office operated without prior approval, in violation of the non-transferability rule.
alac.basis: Article 29 of the Labor Code provides that no license shall be used at any place other than that stated in the license, and that any transfer of business address, appointment of any agent or representative, including the establishment of additional offices anywhere, shall be subject to the prior approval of the Department of Labor (now the Department of Migrant Workers for overseas recruitment).
alac.application: Here, the agency's license covers its Manila office. The Davao office and its agent were not approved, so recruitment there was outside the scope of the license.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Davao activity violated Article 29 and may expose the agency to suspension or cancellation, and the unapproved agent to liability for illegal recruitment.

keyPoints: Non-transferability and place restriction (Art. 29)
Additional offices need prior approval
Unapproved recruitment may be illegal
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 29; RA 8042, as amended

q: Under RA 11641, the power to regulate the recruitment and deployment of OFWs, including suspending or cancelling licenses of overseas recruitment agencies, belongs to:
choices: The POEA, which still exists unchanged
hints: The POEA was absorbed by the DMW.
Administrative cases are separate from criminal cases.
why: RA 11641 created the DMW, which absorbed the POEA's functions, including regulating recruitment, licensing, and suspending or cancelling licenses of overseas agencies for violations, after due process.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 35; Department of Migrant Workers Act (RA 11641), Sec. 6

q: After investigation and hearing, the DMW suspended an overseas recruitment agency's license for deploying workers to a country under a deployment ban. The agency argues that only the POEA could suspend it. Is the agency correct?

alac.answer: No, the DMW validly suspended the license.
alac.basis: RA 11641 created the Department of Migrant Workers and empowered it, among others, to regulate the recruitment, employment and deployment of overseas Filipino workers, absorbing the functions of the POEA, including the power under Article 35 of the Labor Code to suspend or cancel licenses for violations of laws and rules.
alac.application: Here, the agency deployed workers in violation of a deployment ban, a serious violation. The DMW, as successor to the POEA, has the power to suspend its license after due process.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the suspension is valid.

keyPoints: DMW created by RA 11641
Absorbed POEA functions, including licensing powers
Suspension or cancellation for violations after due process
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 35; Department of Migrant Workers Act (RA 11641), Sec. 6

q: Under Article 18 of the Labor Code, direct hiring of Filipino workers for overseas employment is:
choices: Prohibited, except for members of the diplomatic corps, international organizations and other employers allowed by the Secretary
hints: The ban protects workers from abuse.
There are listed exemptions.
why: Labor Code Art. 18 bans direct hiring of Filipinos for overseas work except through authorized entities, with exemptions for diplomatic corps, international organizations, and employers allowed by the Secretary (now DMW rules).
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 18

q: A private company in Qatar directly hired a Filipino engineer through an online interview, without going through any licensed agency or the DMW. Later, a UN agency in Geneva directly hired another Filipino. Are these direct hirings allowed?

alac.answer: The private company's direct hiring is not allowed (unless exempted by DMW rules), but the UN agency's is.
alac.basis: Article 18 of the Labor Code provides that no employer may hire a Filipino worker for overseas employment except through the Boards and entities authorized by the Secretary of Labor, and that direct hiring by members of the diplomatic corps, international organizations and such other employers as may be allowed by the Secretary of Labor is exempted.
alac.application: Here, the Qatar company is a private employer that hired directly without going through authorized channels, which the ban prohibits unless it falls under an exemption allowed by the DMW. The UN agency is an international organization, which is expressly exempt.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the Qatar hiring violates the ban (the worker's deployment should be processed through proper channels), while the UN hiring is allowed.

keyPoints: Ban on direct hiring (Art. 18)
Exemptions: diplomatic corps, international organizations, others allowed
Deployment through authorized channels
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 18

q: Under Article 34 of the Labor Code, which is a prohibited practice?
choices: Charging or accepting any amount greater than the schedule of allowable fees
hints: Prohibited practices apply to licensees too.
Contract substitution is a common violation.
why: Labor Code Art. 34 lists prohibited practices (excessive fees, false notices, misrepresentation, inducing workers to quit, contract substitution, etc.); they are punishable even if committed by licensees, and when done by non-licensees they constitute illegal recruitment (Art. 38).
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 34

q: A licensed agency made an OFW sign a contract for a $1,000 monthly salary, approved by the government, but upon arrival abroad the OFW was made to sign a new contract for $500. What violation, if any, was committed?

alac.answer: The agency committed a prohibited practice, contract substitution, which also constitutes illegal recruitment under RA 8042, as amended.
alac.basis: Article 34 of the Labor Code lists prohibited practices, including substituting or altering employment contracts approved and verified by the Department of Labor from the time of actual signing thereof by the parties up to and including the period of expiration of the same without the approval of the Department. RA 8042, as amended, treats such acts, whether committed by a licensee or a non-licensee, as illegal recruitment.
alac.application: Here, the approved $1,000 contract was replaced abroad with a $500 contract without government approval, which is contract substitution.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the agency is liable for the prohibited practice of contract substitution, which also constitutes illegal recruitment, and the OFW may recover the salary differential.

keyPoints: Prohibited practices (Art. 34)
Contract substitution
Illegal recruitment even by licensees under RA 8042, as amended
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 34

q: Under Article 38 of the Labor Code and RA 8042, as amended, illegal recruitment is considered an offense involving economic sabotage when committed:
choices: By a syndicate (three or more persons conspiring) or in large scale (against three or more persons)
By one person against one victim
hints: Simple, syndicated or large-scale.
Elements: recruitment activity plus lack of license (for non-licensees).
why: Illegal recruitment: (1) recruitment activities by a non-licensee or non-holder of authority; (2) for overseas employment, also certain prohibited acts by anyone. It involves economic sabotage when committed by a syndicate (three or more conspirators) or in large scale (three or more victims), with heavier penalties.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 38; RA 8042, as amended, Sec. 6

q: Without any license, Dina and Ella promised overseas jobs to four applicants and collected fees from each. No one was deployed. What crime did they commit?

alac.answer: They committed illegal recruitment in large scale, an offense involving economic sabotage.
alac.basis: Article 38 of the Labor Code provides that any recruitment activities undertaken by non-licensees or non-holders of authority shall be deemed illegal, and that illegal recruitment committed by a syndicate or in large scale is an offense involving economic sabotage; it is in large scale if committed against three or more persons individually or as a group. RA 8042, as amended, likewise defines and penalizes illegal recruitment for overseas employment.
alac.application: Here, Dina and Ella, who had no license, promised overseas jobs and collected fees, which is recruitment. They did so against four persons, three or more.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, they are liable for illegal recruitment in large scale (not syndicated, since there were only two of them), punished as economic sabotage.

keyPoints: Illegal recruitment by non-licensees (Art. 38)
Large scale: three or more victims
Syndicated: three or more conspirators
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 38; RA 8042, as amended, Sec. 6

q: According to People v. Ochoa, a person convicted of illegal recruitment may also be convicted of estafa for the same acts because:
choices: Illegal recruitment is malum prohibitum while estafa is malum in se, with different elements
hints: Different elements: no double jeopardy.
Good faith is no defense to illegal recruitment.
why: Illegal recruitment (malum prohibitum, intent immaterial) and estafa (malum in se, requiring deceit and damage) have different elements, so a person may be convicted of both for the same acts without double jeopardy (People v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 173792, August 31, 2011).
cite: People v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 173792, August 31, 2011; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 38

q: Fely, unlicensed, falsely told an applicant she could deploy him to Japan, and he paid her P80,000. She was convicted of illegal recruitment. Can she also be convicted of estafa for the same acts?

alac.answer: Yes, Fely may also be convicted of estafa.
alac.basis: In People v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 173792, August 31, 2011, the Supreme Court held that a person may be charged and convicted separately of illegal recruitment and estafa for the same acts, because illegal recruitment is malum prohibitum, where criminal intent is not necessary, while estafa is malum in se, which requires deceit and damage, so the two crimes have different elements and double jeopardy does not apply. Article 38 of the Labor Code penalizes recruitment by non-licensees.
alac.application: Here, Fely recruited without a license, which is illegal recruitment. She also falsely represented that she could deploy the applicant, inducing him to pay P80,000, which is deceit causing damage, the elements of estafa.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, Fely may be convicted of both illegal recruitment and estafa.

keyPoints: Illegal recruitment is malum prohibitum
Estafa is malum in se with deceit and damage
Conviction for both allowed (People v. Ochoa)
cite: People v. Ochoa, G.R. No. 173792, August 31, 2011; Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Art. 38

q: Under Articles 36 and 37 of the Labor Code, the Secretary of Labor has, over entities engaged in recruitment:
choices: Regulatory power to restrict and regulate recruitment, and visitorial power to inspect premises, books and records
hints: Inspection may be done at any time.
Local recruitment remains with the DOLE.
why: Labor Code Art. 36: regulatory power to restrict and regulate recruitment and issue rules; Art. 37: visitorial power to inspect premises, books and records and act on violations; the DOLE retains these over local recruitment, while the DMW handles overseas recruitment.
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Arts. 36-37

q: A local employment agency refused to let DOLE inspectors examine its records, saying the inspectors needed a search warrant. Is the agency correct?

alac.answer: No, the agency must allow the inspection.
alac.basis: Article 37 of the Labor Code provides that the Secretary of Labor or his duly authorized representatives may, at any time, inspect the premises, books of accounts and records of any person or entity covered by the Title on recruitment, require it to submit reports, and act on violations. Article 36 gives the Secretary regulatory power over recruitment agencies. Licensed agencies, being in a regulated business, are subject to such administrative inspections.
alac.application: Here, the agency is a local employment agency covered by the Title. The DOLE inspectors are exercising the Secretary's visitorial power, for which a search warrant is not required in this regulated business.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, the agency must allow the inspection, and its refusal may be a ground for sanctions.

keyPoints: Regulatory power (Art. 36)
Visitorial power to inspect at any time (Art. 37)
Applies to regulated recruitment businesses
cite: Labor Code (PD 442, as amended), Arts. 36-37

q: Under RA 11641, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) is mandated to:
choices: Formulate and implement policies for the protection of OFWs and regulate their recruitment, employment and deployment
hints: The DMW absorbed the POEA.
Money claims of OFWs remain with the NLRC labor arbiters.
why: RA 11641 created the DMW as the primary agency for OFW protection, absorbing the POEA and other offices; it regulates overseas recruitment and deployment, adjudicates certain administrative cases, and coordinates assistance to OFWs.
cite: Department of Migrant Workers Act (RA 11641), Sec. 6

q: An OFW who was maltreated by her employer in Kuwait asks which government department is primarily responsible for her protection and for regulating the agency that deployed her. Advise her.

alac.answer: The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) is primarily responsible.
alac.basis: RA 11641 created the Department of Migrant Workers and mandated it to formulate, recommend, and implement national policies, plans, programs, and guidelines that will ensure the protection of OFWs, and to regulate the recruitment, employment and deployment of OFWs, absorbing the functions of the POEA and related offices. Money claims arising from employer-employee relations remain within the jurisdiction of the labor arbiters under RA 8042, as amended.
alac.application: Here, the OFW needs protection and assistance abroad and wants action against the deploying agency. The DMW is the department primarily responsible for both.
alac.conclusion: Therefore, she may seek assistance from the DMW and file administrative complaints against the agency there, and file her money claims with the NLRC labor arbiter.

keyPoints: DMW created by RA 11641
Mandate to protect OFWs and regulate recruitment
Money claims with labor arbiters
cite: Department of Migrant Workers Act (RA 11641), Sec. 6
